primary_text: When household income is limited, essential expenses compete for the same dollars. Food is one of the few expenses that can often be reduced quickly when money becomes tight.
secondary_text: Low income increases vulnerability to food insecurity, but benefits, savings, household structure, and local costs can change how strongly one affects the other.

primary_text: Job loss or unstable employment can reduce household income and make food budgets less predictable, increasing the chance that a household cannot consistently afford enough food.
secondary_text: Unemployment does not automatically produce food insecurity. Savings, benefits, other household income, and local living costs can buffer or amplify the effect.

primary_text: Rent, utilities, and food all compete for limited household resources. When housing costs become unaffordable, families may have less money available for groceries.
secondary_text: Housing instability can affect health indirectly because households may be forced to choose between rent, utilities, food, medicines, and transportation.

primary_text: Diet choices depend on what is realistically available. Price, distance, transportation, store selection, and time can all limit access to nutritious foods.
secondary_text: Improving individual nutrition knowledge cannot fully solve a food environment where nutritious choices are unaffordable or difficult to reach.

primary_text: Food insecurity can change both what people eat and when they eat. Cheaper, shelf-stable foods may become more practical when money or food availability is uncertain.
secondary_text: Food insecurity and diet quality overlap, but they are not the same thing. A person can experience food insecurity without having the same dietary pattern as another household.

primary_text: Physical activity is shaped partly by the environment. Unsafe streets, poor sidewalks, long distances, limited parks, and recreation costs can make routine movement harder.
secondary_text: Physical inactivity is not simply a matter of motivation. The built environment can either make movement convenient and safe or make it substantially harder.

primary_text: Diet patterns influence total energy intake, satiety, and metabolic health. Over time, some eating patterns can contribute to excess weight, although body weight has many influences.
secondary_text: Body weight is influenced by many interacting factors, including genetics, medications, sleep, stress, activity, food environment, and socioeconomic conditions.

primary_text: Physical activity helps muscles take up glucose and improves insulin sensitivity. Lower activity can contribute to poorer glucose regulation and higher Type 2 diabetes risk.
secondary_text: The Diabetes Prevention Program found that a combined lifestyle program involving activity, dietary change, and modest weight loss substantially reduced progression to Type 2 diabetes.
statistic_text: In the NIH Diabetes Prevention Program, a combined lifestyle program involving physical activity, dietary change, and modest weight loss lowered the chance of developing type 2 diabetes by 58% versus placebo after about 3 years. This does not isolate physical activity by itself.

primary_text: Excess body fat, particularly visceral fat, is associated with metabolic changes that can impair insulin action and increase the likelihood of Type 2 diabetes.
secondary_text: Body size alone does not determine whether someone will develop diabetes. Genetics, age, activity, fat distribution, and other metabolic factors also matter.

primary_text: Adipose tissue is biologically active. Excess visceral fat can alter inflammatory and hormonal signaling in ways that make cells less responsive to insulin.
secondary_text: Insulin resistance is one of the major biological links between excess adiposity and Type 2 diabetes.

primary_text: When cells respond poorly to insulin, the pancreas initially compensates by producing more insulin. Over time, that compensation may become insufficient and glucose begins to rise.
secondary_text: Elevated glucose may begin before a person feels symptoms, which is why screening can identify metabolic problems earlier.

primary_text: Type 2 diabetes develops when glucose regulation becomes persistently abnormal. Rising glucose often develops gradually as insulin resistance and impaired insulin production progress.
secondary_text: Prediabetes and elevated glucose can create an important window for lifestyle support, monitoring, and prevention before Type 2 diabetes develops.

primary_text: When blood glucose becomes high enough, the kidneys remove more glucose through urine. Water follows the glucose, increasing fluid loss and triggering stronger thirst.
secondary_text: The combination of fluid loss and frequent urination can leave someone feeling unusually thirsty even after drinking.

primary_text: Excess glucose in the urine pulls water with it. That increases urine production, which can make someone urinate more frequently than usual.
secondary_text: Frequent urination can have many causes, so the symptom by itself does not establish a diabetes diagnosis.

primary_text: Diabetes can contribute to fatigue through impaired glucose regulation, dehydration, sleep disruption, and other related health problems.
secondary_text: Fatigue is highly nonspecific. Diabetes is one possible cause among many and persistent fatigue needs broader clinical context.

primary_text: Changes in blood glucose can temporarily alter fluid levels inside the eye and affect focusing. Diabetes can also damage retinal blood vessels over time.
secondary_text: Persistent or sudden vision changes deserve evaluation because blurred vision may reflect temporary glucose changes or a more serious eye problem.

primary_text: Long-term high blood glucose can damage nerves as well as the small blood vessels that supply them, leading to numbness, tingling, pain, or loss of sensation.
secondary_text: Loss of sensation is particularly important because injuries may occur without pain, increasing the risk of unnoticed wounds.

primary_text: Persistently elevated blood glucose can damage the small blood vessels and filtering structures in the kidneys. Damage may progress for years before symptoms appear.
secondary_text: Kidney disease can be present without obvious symptoms, making blood and urine screening important for early detection.
statistic_text: Approximately 1 in 3 adults with diabetes has chronic kidney disease.

primary_text: Diabetes can damage blood vessels and commonly occurs alongside high blood pressure and abnormal cholesterol, increasing cardiovascular risk.
secondary_text: People with diabetes have substantially higher cardiovascular risk than people without diabetes.
statistic_text: People with diabetes have about twice the risk of heart disease compared with people without diabetes.

primary_text: Diabetes affects blood vessels and often clusters with other stroke risk factors such as high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol, and cardiovascular disease.
secondary_text: Diabetes is an established stroke risk factor, especially when combined with high blood pressure or cardiovascular disease.
statistic_text: People with diabetes are about twice as likely to have heart disease or a stroke as people without diabetes.

primary_text: High blood glucose can damage tiny blood vessels in the retina. Early diabetic eye disease may develop without noticeable changes in vision.
secondary_text: Regular eye examinations can detect diabetic eye disease before a person notices vision loss.

primary_text: Nerve damage can reduce sensation in the feet while poor circulation can impair healing. Small injuries may therefore go unnoticed and become more serious.
secondary_text: Early identification and treatment of foot injuries can prevent minor wounds from progressing to infection or more serious complications.

primary_text: Access to care affects screening, diagnosis, medication, preventive counseling, and ongoing disease management. Delayed or fragmented care can allow risk to go unrecognized.
secondary_text: Healthcare access is broader than insurance. Provider supply, transportation, affordability, language, trust, and appointment availability can all affect access.

primary_text: Food insecurity can affect diabetes risk through several pathways at once: diet quality, irregular eating, chronic stress, financial strain, and difficulty maintaining preventive care.
secondary_text: Food insecurity is strongly associated with Type 2 diabetes at the population level, but the relationship operates through multiple pathways rather than one simple direct cause.

primary_text: Lower physical activity can reduce energy expenditure and influence energy balance, making weight gain more likely for some people over time.
secondary_text: Physical inactivity can contribute to weight gain but does not determine body weight on its own. Diet, biology, medications, sleep, stress, and environment also matter.

primary_text: Higher sodium intake can cause the body to retain more fluid and can increase blood pressure. Salt sensitivity differs across people, so the size of the effect is not identical for everyone.
secondary_text: Most sodium in the U.S. diet comes from packaged, processed, and restaurant foods, so sodium exposure is influenced by the food environment as well as individual choices.

primary_text: Regular physical activity helps the heart and blood vessels function efficiently and can lower blood pressure. Low activity is therefore one of the modifiable factors associated with hypertension risk.
secondary_text: Physical activity can lower blood pressure even when body weight does not change dramatically, so its effect is not only through weight loss.

primary_text: Having overweight or obesity can increase the workload on the heart and is associated with biological changes that make high blood pressure more likely.
secondary_text: Body weight does not determine blood pressure by itself. Genetics, age, diet, activity, sleep, medicines, kidney function, and other factors also matter.

primary_text: Stress activates nervous-system and hormonal responses that can temporarily raise blood pressure. When stress is persistent, repeated activation and stress-related behaviors may contribute to longer-term hypertension risk.
secondary_text: Stress does not automatically cause chronic hypertension. The relationship is complex and depends on duration, coping resources, other exposures, and health behaviors.

primary_text: Hypertension often has no symptoms, so prevention and control depend on screening, reliable follow-up, medication access when needed, and ongoing support. Barriers to care can interfere at each of those steps.
secondary_text: Because high blood pressure is often silent, missed screening or interrupted care can leave it untreated even when a person feels completely well.

primary_text: Persistently high pressure can damage arteries and place extra strain on the heart. Over time, this increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, including heart attack and heart failure.
secondary_text: Blood pressure control is a major part of preventing cardiovascular events in people who already have other metabolic risks such as diabetes.

primary_text: High blood pressure damages and weakens blood vessels and is one of the most important modifiable risk factors for stroke.
secondary_text: Treating high blood pressure is one of the clearest ways to reduce preventable stroke risk at the population and individual level.

primary_text: High pressure can damage the small blood vessels in the kidneys, reducing their ability to filter blood effectively. Kidney disease can also worsen blood pressure, creating a two-way relationship.
secondary_text: The kidney relationship runs in both directions: hypertension can damage the kidneys, while chronic kidney disease can also cause or worsen hypertension.
statistic_text: About 1 in 5 adults with high blood pressure has chronic kidney disease.

primary_text: Diabetes and hypertension frequently occur together. Diabetes is a recognized risk factor for high blood pressure, and the combination substantially increases cardiovascular and kidney risk.
secondary_text: This is a risk relationship, not a guarantee. Many people with diabetes do not develop hypertension, and hypertension also occurs without diabetes.

primary_text: When affordable housing choices are limited, households may have fewer options to leave or repair homes with leaks, dampness, mold, pests, or other environmental hazards.
secondary_text: Housing instability does not mean that a home has mold. The pathway reflects increased exposure risk through substandard housing conditions, not a deterministic relationship.

primary_text: Outdoor air pollution can irritate inflamed airways. Ozone, particle pollution, traffic emissions, and wildfire smoke can worsen symptoms and provoke attacks in some people with asthma.
secondary_text: Air quality is partly a community-level exposure. People can reduce exposure on bad-air days, but they cannot individually control regional pollution or wildfire smoke.

primary_text: Mold grows where moisture is present. In people with asthma who are sensitive to mold, breathing mold spores can worsen symptoms or trigger an attack.
secondary_text: Controlling moisture, repairing leaks, drying wet materials, and safely remediating mold address the exposure itself rather than only treating symptoms.

primary_text: Secondhand tobacco smoke contains airway irritants that can trigger asthma attacks and make asthma harder to control.
secondary_text: Smoke-free homes, vehicles, workplaces, and public spaces can reduce exposure even when the person with asthma does not smoke.

primary_text: Indoor allergens such as dust mites, cockroach or pest allergens, and pet dander can trigger symptoms in people who are sensitive to them.
secondary_text: Not every person with asthma reacts to the same allergens. Trigger-control strategies should be matched to the person and the exposures actually present.

primary_text: Strong emotions and stress can change breathing patterns and may worsen asthma symptoms in some people.
secondary_text: Stress is one possible trigger, not the cause of every asthma attack. Environmental exposures, infections, allergens, and treatment factors may also contribute.

primary_text: Good asthma control depends on diagnosis, appropriate medicines, inhaler education, an asthma action plan, and follow-up with a health care professional.
secondary_text: Insurance, medication cost, transportation, clinician availability, language, and continuity of care can all affect whether asthma treatment is realistic to maintain.

primary_text: Asthma symptoms can worsen suddenly or gradually into an exacerbation, when airway inflammation and narrowing make breathing more difficult.
secondary_text: An asthma action plan helps people recognize worsening symptoms, use prescribed treatment appropriately, and know when urgent care is needed.

primary_text: Narrowed airways can create turbulent airflow that produces a whistling or squeaking sound, especially when breathing out.
secondary_text: Wheezing is common in asthma but is not specific to asthma and can occur with other respiratory conditions.

primary_text: Airway narrowing and inflammation can make it harder to move air, producing a feeling of breathlessness or difficulty breathing.
secondary_text: Severe or rapidly worsening breathing difficulty can be an emergency and should be handled according to the person’s asthma action plan and clinical guidance.

primary_text: When asthma narrows and inflames the airways, some people experience pressure or tightness in the chest.
secondary_text: Chest symptoms have many possible causes, so persistent, severe, or unusual chest symptoms need appropriate clinical evaluation.

primary_text: Asthma can cause recurrent cough as inflamed, sensitive airways react to triggers. Cough may be especially noticeable at night or early in the morning.
secondary_text: Cough is very common and has many causes. Its pattern and relationship to other asthma symptoms and triggers are important.

primary_text: Obesity is associated with increased asthma risk and can make asthma symptoms more difficult to control. The biological pathways are complex and vary among individuals.
secondary_text: Body weight alone does not determine who develops asthma. Genetics, allergies, infections, environmental exposures, and other factors also contribute.

primary_text: Dietary fat quality can influence blood lipid levels, especially LDL cholesterol.
secondary_text: High cholesterol also reflects genetics, age, medical conditions, and medication effects—not diet alone.

primary_text: Physical inactivity is one of the modifiable behaviors associated with high cholesterol risk.
secondary_text: Activity affects cholesterol partly through body weight and metabolism, so the pathway is not identical for every person.

primary_text: Higher body weight can shift lipid metabolism toward a more atherogenic profile.
secondary_text: The relationship is population-level and does not mean every person with obesity has high cholesterol.

primary_text: Diabetes can lower HDL and raise LDL-related cardiovascular risk.
secondary_text: Managing glucose and lipids together is important because the conditions often cluster.

primary_text: Excess atherogenic cholesterol can accumulate in artery walls and contribute to atherosclerotic plaque.
secondary_text: Lowering LDL cholesterol can reduce cardiovascular risk, especially in people at elevated baseline risk.

primary_text: Plaque buildup in arteries can increase the chance of vascular blockage that contributes to ischemic stroke.
secondary_text: Stroke has multiple causes; cholesterol is one modifiable risk factor among several.

primary_text: Chronically elevated blood pressure damages arteries and increases atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk.
secondary_text: Blood-pressure control is one of the major preventable pathways for reducing heart disease risk.

primary_text: Diabetes accelerates vascular damage and commonly occurs with other cardiovascular risk factors.
secondary_text: Cardiovascular prevention is a central part of long-term diabetes care.

primary_text: Tobacco smoke damages blood vessels, promotes atherosclerosis, and increases clotting risk.
secondary_text: Stopping smoking lowers cardiovascular risk even after years of tobacco exposure.
statistic_text: CDC estimates that cigarette smoking raises coronary heart disease risk about 2 to 4 times compared with not smoking.

primary_text: Regular activity helps improve blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose regulation, and cardiovascular fitness.
secondary_text: Activity works through several pathways rather than a single direct mechanism.

primary_text: Excess body weight is linked with hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, and direct cardiovascular strain.
secondary_text: Risk depends on multiple factors; body weight alone does not determine whether CHD develops.

primary_text: When heart muscle receives too little oxygen-rich blood, chest pain or pressure can occur.
secondary_text: New or severe chest pain can be an emergency and should not be interpreted from this graph alone.

primary_text: A heart attack occurs when coronary blood flow is blocked long enough to damage heart muscle.
secondary_text: Rapid emergency treatment is critical when a heart attack occurs.

primary_text: Repeated tobacco smoke exposure damages airways and lung tissue over time.
secondary_text: COPD can occur in people who never smoked; occupational, environmental, genetic, and early-life factors also contribute.
statistic_text: Cigarette smoking contributes to as many as 8 in 10 COPD-related deaths in the United States.

primary_text: Inhaling tobacco smoke from other people exposes the lungs to many of the same harmful chemicals.
secondary_text: Reducing secondhand smoke protects both people with COPD and people at risk of developing it.

primary_text: Repeated inhalation of workplace respiratory hazards can contribute to chronic airway and lung damage.
secondary_text: Risk varies by exposure intensity, duration, protective controls, and smoking history.

primary_text: Air pollution can irritate already vulnerable airways and worsen respiratory symptoms in people with COPD, increasing the chance of a flare or exacerbation.
secondary_text: Poor air quality can also contribute to respiratory disease risk, but this arrow is intentionally drawn to COPD exacerbations because worsening of established COPD is the clearest relationship represented here.

primary_text: Chronic airway disease earlier in life can be associated with persistent airflow limitation later on.
secondary_text: Asthma and COPD are distinct conditions and can also coexist.

primary_text: COPD can increase airway irritation and mucus production, leading to persistent cough.
secondary_text: A chronic cough has many possible causes and is not specific to COPD.

primary_text: Airflow limitation makes it harder to move air in and out of the lungs, particularly during activity.
secondary_text: Breathlessness can substantially limit daily activity and quality of life.

primary_text: Exacerbations are episodes of acute symptom worsening that may require additional treatment or hospitalization.
secondary_text: Preventing exacerbations is a major goal of COPD management.

primary_text: Tobacco smoke contains carcinogens that damage DNA and can cause cancer in multiple organs.
secondary_text: This relationship applies to many—but not every—cancer type.
statistic_text: Cigarette smoking causes about 1 out of every 3 cancer deaths in the United States.

primary_text: Alcohol use raises the risk of several cancers, including cancers of the mouth, throat, larynx, esophagus, colon and rectum, liver, and breast.
secondary_text: The broad Cancer node represents a group of diseases; this arrow does not imply that alcohol raises risk for every cancer type.
statistic_text: NCI estimates alcohol consumption was responsible for about 5% of U.S. cancer cases in 2019. Risk varies greatly by cancer type and drinking level.

primary_text: Overweight and obesity are associated with increased risk of multiple cancer types through pathways that can include inflammation, insulin signaling, and hormone changes.
secondary_text: This relationship applies to specific cancer types and should not be interpreted as a universal cancer pathway.
statistic_text: Overweight and obesity are associated with higher risk of 13 cancer types; together, those cancers make up about 40% of cancers diagnosed in the United States each year. This does not mean excess weight causes 40% of all cancers.

primary_text: Regular physical activity is associated with lower risk of several cancer types; lower activity therefore corresponds with higher risk for those cancers.
secondary_text: The association varies by cancer type and does not imply that inactivity causes every cancer.

primary_text: Cancer itself and cancer treatments can cause cancer-related fatigue, which can be persistent and interfere with daily functioning.
secondary_text: Fatigue is common in cancer care but is nonspecific and can also result from anemia, sleep problems, pain, depression, medicines, and other conditions.
statistic_text: More than 80% of people with cancer experience fatigue while receiving chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Fatigue can also occur from the cancer itself and other treatments.

primary_text: Long-term stress has been linked with depression and can affect sleep, coping, mood, and stress-response systems.
secondary_text: Depression is multifactorial. Stress exposure does not mean a person will develop depression.

primary_text: Lower social connection and social isolation are associated with higher depression risk across multiple populations.
secondary_text: The relationship can operate in both directions: depression may also make social connection harder.

primary_text: Systematic reviews find that unemployment is associated with higher risk of depressive symptoms and major depression.
secondary_text: Health selection and other social and economic factors can contribute, so this is represented as an association rather than a deterministic pathway.

primary_text: Housing insecurity and housing disadvantage are associated with worse mental health and depressive symptoms, especially when instability or unaffordable housing persists.
secondary_text: Evidence is largely observational and definitions of housing insecurity vary, so the arrow represents an association rather than proof of a single causal mechanism.

primary_text: People with chronic diseases such as diabetes have a higher risk of depression, and depression can also make chronic-disease management more difficult.
secondary_text: This is a bidirectional association, not a claim that diabetes inevitably causes depression.

primary_text: Some people with cancer have a higher risk of depression because of illness burden, treatment effects, stress, and other biological and psychosocial factors.
secondary_text: Depression is not an inevitable response to cancer and should be evaluated and treated as its own condition.

primary_text: Depression can change sleep duration, timing, and quality, including insomnia or sleeping too much.
secondary_text: Sleep problems can also worsen mood, creating a reinforcing cycle.

primary_text: Depression can affect attention, processing speed, memory, and decision-making.
secondary_text: Cognitive symptoms can interfere with school, work, and treatment follow-through.

primary_text: Depression can produce persistent tiredness and reduced energy even when physical exertion is limited.
secondary_text: Fatigue is nonspecific and should not be assumed to be caused by depression without evaluation.

primary_text: Depression treatment may involve psychotherapy, medication, or both, which require accessible and sustained care.
secondary_text: Barriers such as cost, transportation, clinician availability, stigma, and insurance can interrupt treatment.
